page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.A2.Flex.4-32 is a flexible general-purpose virtual machine based on the arm64 architecture. The instance is powered by Ampere AmpereOne processors operating at a nominal clock frequency of 3.0 GHz. It is provisioned with 8 dedicated physical cores mapped directly to 8 vCPUs at a ratio of one thread per core, preventing execution jitter commonly introduced by simultaneous multithreading. System memory is sized at 32.0 GB of RAM, yielding an even distribution of 4.0 GB per physical core.

The VM.Standard.A2.Flex.4-32 configuration does not include local storage devices, necessitating remote block storage attachments for operating system installation and persistent data management. GPU accelerators are not present. Network connectivity is supported with one complimentary public IPv4 address. The provision of dedicated, non-hyperthreaded cores offers consistent compute behavior and resource density without the performance penalties of shared processor capacity. This profile aligns with general cloud tasks including containerized application runtimes, web serving tiers, software build runners, and microservices.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.A2.Flex.4-32 is an arm64-based virtual machine configured with 8 vCPUs and 32.0 GB of system memory. Powered by 3.0 GHz Ampere AmpereOne processors, the instance allocates 8 dedicated physical cores with a single thread per core, providing predictable execution without multi-threading contention. With a balanced allocation of 4.0 GB of RAM per core, the shape adheres to a standard 1:4 compute-to-memory profile. The instance includes no integrated local storage or GPU accelerators, relying on remote block storage for data persistence, while offering one complimentary public IPv4 address. Its dedicated core architecture delivers steady compute throughput and favorable resource density relative to operational overhead. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.A2.Flex.4-32 is structured for general-purpose server workloads, such as web applications, container clusters, microservices, and continuous integration pipelines.
